chapter_title: Day 2: Byzantine Constantinople and Hagia Sophia
learning_objective: The learner will classify ten statements about Byzantine Constantinople as a primary source, a myth, contested history, or settled history, classifying at least 8 of 10 correctly on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** source-myth-or-contested
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify ten statements about Byzantine Constantinople as a primary source, a myth, contested history, or settled history, classifying at least 8 of 10 correctly on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** primary source, secondary source, myth, history, contested history (all defined in Part One, "Whose Story Is This?", above). **Evidence of Mastery:** For each statement, the learner chooses one of four categories before seeing feedback. An answer is correct when it matches the Correct category column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. **Misconceptions:** (1) A primary source is a true source. (2) A myth is a lie and has no value. (3) Any disagreement means the facts are unknown, when in contested history the facts are agreed and the meaning is disputed. (4) A story told by every tour guide must be history. **Instructional Rationale:** Classifying real statements from the day's sites forces the learner to apply the three definitions to the kind of claim they will actually hear in Hagia Sophia, rather than to textbook examples. Immediate feedback with the reason corrects each misconception at the moment it appears. **Content:** The four categories, shown with these one-line definitions: - Primary source: evidence written or made at the time, by someone who was there or close to it. - Myth: a story first recorded long after the event, with no support from the time. - Contested history: the facts are agreed, but their meaning or proper use is disputed today. - Settled history: a fact agreed by the sources and by modern historians. | # | Statement shown to the learner | Correct category | Reason shown after answering | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Procopius, writing in the 550s for Justinian, says the dome seems to hang from heaven by a golden chain. | Primary source | Procopius saw the building new; his praise was written for the emperor, so we read it with that purpose in mind. | | 2 | On entering the finished church, Justinian cried, "Solomon, I have outdone thee!" | Myth | The line first appears in the *Diēgēsis*, written about three hundred years later; Procopius and Paul the Silentiary do not mention it. | | 3 | Hagia Sophia was dedicated in December 537. | Settled history | The date is agreed by the sources of the time and by modern historians. | | 4 | The green marble columns in Hagia Sophia were taken from the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. | Myth | It is a later tradition with no support from the 6th century; the stone is a green marble quarried in Thessaly, in Greece. | | 5 | Procopius, who lived through the Nika Riots, says more than 30,000 people were killed in the Hippodrome. | Primary source | It is an eyewitness-era number from one writer; the figure may be exaggerated, but the source is from the time. | | 6 | Hagia Sophia should be a mosque today. | Contested history | The dates of its conversions are agreed; whether it should be a mosque, a church, or a museum is a disagreement about values. | | 7 | The Medusa heads in the Basilica Cistern were set upside down to cancel the gaze of the Gorgon. | Myth | No source from the time explains their position; using them as column bases to make up the height is the simpler explanation. | | 8 | Niketas Choniates, a Byzantine official, wrote that crusaders seated a woman on the patriarch's throne in Hagia Sophia in 1204. | Primary source | Choniates lived through the sack; he was a bitter victim, so his account is vivid and one-sided. | | 9 | The army of the Fourth Crusade captured and sacked Constantinople in April 1204. | Settled history | Byzantine and crusader sources agree on the event and its date. | | 10 | The four bronze horses taken from the Hippodrome in 1204 belong in Venice. | Contested history | Where the horses came from is agreed; who should keep them today is a matter of opinion. | **Provenance:** Statements 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 to 10 come from Part One and Part Seven of this chapter. Statement 4 comes from Part Two ("Spolia"); statement 7 from Part Five ("Medusa Heads"). **Rules:** Each statement is answered once for scoring. A first-attempt answer is correct if and only if it equals the Correct category. Score is the count of correct first attempts, 0 to 10. Mastery is score >= 8. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner reads the four category definitions. 2. The learner sees statement 1 and chooses a category. 3. Feedback appears; the learner moves to the next statement. 4. After statement 10, the learner sees their score and a list of any statements they missed, each with its reason. 5. The learner should notice that two statements by eyewitnesses (1 and 8) are primary sources even though each is one-sided. **Feedback:** Statements appear in the order listed. After each first attempt, the sim shows "Correct" or "Not quite: this is [correct category]", followed by the reason from the table. The learner may not change a scored answer. At the end: score >= 8 shows "You can tell a source from a story. That skill works at every stop on this trip."; score < 8 shows "Try the set again; watch for who wrote each statement and when." A Try Again option reshuffles the order of the same ten statements. **Starting State:** The four category definitions and statement 1, with the question "What kind of statement is this?" **Chapter Anchors:** Procopius wrote in the 550s; the Solomon line first appears about three hundred years later; Hagia Sophia dedicated December 537; Nika Riots death toll "more than 30,000" per Procopius; sack of April 1204; ten statements; mastery 8 of 10.
